# How to use this guide

Medicinal Chemistry I is a memory subject with a logic behind it. Almost every mark comes from four things: **classification**, **structure–activity relationship (SAR)**, **mechanism of action with uses**, and the **synthesis of the starred drugs**. Work unit by unit: read the notes, write the SAR points as a labelled skeleton from memory, then write each starred synthesis as a numbered scheme without looking. Finish the unit with the question bank and the MCQs.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ or very short answers | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; learn the full answer with the structure skeleton, the SAR points and one synthesis.
- **Medium** — asked every few years, or as a part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for the objective section and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from syllabus weight and common patterns in pharmacy papers, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Introduction | Physicochemical properties (ionization, partition coefficient, protein binding, chelation), bioisosterism with examples, phase I and phase II metabolism with reactions, factors affecting metabolism |
| 2 Adrenergic | Biosynthesis and catabolism of catecholamines, SAR of sympathomimetics, SAR of beta blockers, classification of adrenergic antagonists, synthesis of phenylephrine, salbutamol, tolazoline, propranolol |
| 3 Cholinergic | Biosynthesis of acetylcholine, SAR of parasympathomimetics, mechanism of anticholinesterases and pralidoxime, SAR and classification of anticholinergics, synthesis of carbachol, neostigmine, ipratropium, dicyclomine, procyclidine |
| 4 CNS I | SAR of benzodiazepines and barbiturates, SAR of phenothiazines with classification of antipsychotics, SAR and mechanism of anticonvulsants, synthesis of diazepam, barbital, chlorpromazine, phenytoin, ethosuximide, carbamazepine |
| 5 CNS II | Classification of general anaesthetics, SAR of morphine analogues, classification of NSAIDs, synthesis of halothane, methohexital, ketamine, fentanyl, methadone, mefenamic acid, ibuprofen |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. **Draw first, write second.** Start a SAR answer with the labelled skeleton (phenylethylamine, aryloxypropanolamine, benzodiazepine, phenothiazine, barbituric acid, morphine "T"), then number the SAR points against the positions you have marked.
2. **Numbered schemes for synthesis.** Write each step as "reagent → product" with the name of the reaction where it has one (Friedel–Crafts, Mannich, Grignard, Knoevenagel, Ullmann, benzoin condensation, Pinner). Even if you cannot draw the structures neatly, a correct numbered sequence carries most of the marks.
3. **Classification answers should be a table or tree**, with one named example and one use per class. Examiners count the classes, not the adjectives.
4. **Link chemistry to the clinic in every answer.** Say *why* a catechol is inactive orally, *why* a quaternary nitrogen keeps a drug out of the brain, *why* thiopental wears off in minutes.
5. **Keep a drug list per unit** with class, mechanism and one use. Most objective questions are "which class does this drug belong to" or "which drug is the antidote".
6. **Learn the starred drugs cold.** Twenty-two drugs carry an asterisk in this syllabus and they are the most likely 10-mark questions: phenylephrine, salbutamol, tolazoline, propranolol, carbachol, neostigmine, ipratropium bromide, dicyclomine, procyclidine, diazepam, barbital, chlorpromazine, phenytoin, ethosuximide, carbamazepine, halothane, methohexital sodium, ketamine, fentanyl, methadone, mefenamic acid, ibuprofen.
7. **Do not mix up the two SARs that look alike.** Sympathomimetics use a phenylethylamine skeleton (nitrogen substituent decides alpha or beta); anticholinergics need two bulky rings and a cationic nitrogen. Writing one for the other loses the whole question.
8. **For practicals**, remember the reaction type, the melting point range, the recrystallising solvent and the titrant with its equivalence factor. Viva questions come from exactly these four.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you have only an hour, learn these five with full skeletons: **SAR of sympathomimetics**, **SAR of beta blockers**, **SAR of parasympathomimetics and anticholinergics**, **SAR of benzodiazepines, barbiturates and phenothiazines**, and **phase I / phase II metabolism**. Then read the synthesis table below twice.

## The five skeletons to draw from memory

```text
1. Sympathomimetic      Ar(3,4-OH) — CH(OH) — CH(R') — NH — R
                        N-substituent: H→α, CH3→α+β, iPr→β, t-Bu→β2

2. Beta blocker         Ar — O — CH2 — CH(OH) — CH2 — NH — iPr
                        para substituent on benzene → β1 selective; naphthalene → propranolol

3. Acetylcholine        CH3CO — O — CH2CH2 — N+(CH3)3   (five-atom rule)
                        carbamate → resists AChE; β-methyl → muscarinic selectivity

4. Anticholinergic      (Ar)(Ar or cyclohexyl)(OH)C — CO — O — CH2CH2 — N(R)2
                        tertiary → central; quaternary → peripheral only

5. Morphine "T"         aromatic ring + quaternary carbon + 2-carbon bridge + basic N
                        N-CH3 → agonist; N-allyl / N-cyclopropylmethyl → antagonist
```

## Starred syntheses in one line each

| Drug | Route in one line |
| --- | --- |
| Phenylephrine | 3-Hydroxyacetophenone → brominate → N-benzylmethylamine → H2/Pd (reduce + debenzylate) → resolve |
| Salbutamol | Methyl salicylate → Friedel–Crafts acetylation → brominate → N-benzyl-t-butylamine → LiAlH4 → H2/Pd |
| Tolazoline | Benzyl cyanide → imino ether (HCl/EtOH) → ethylenediamine → 2-benzyl-2-imidazoline |
| Propranolol | 1-Naphthol + epichlorohydrin → epoxide → isopropylamine |
| Carbachol | 2-Chloroethanol + phosgene → chloroformate → ammonia → carbamate → trimethylamine |
| Neostigmine | 3-Dimethylaminophenol + dimethylcarbamoyl chloride → quaternise with methyl bromide |
| Ipratropium | Atropine → demethylate (noratropine) → isopropyl bromide → methyl bromide |
| Dicyclomine | Benzyl cyanide + 1,5-dibromopentane → hydrolyse → hydrogenate ring → acid chloride + diethylaminoethanol |
| Procyclidine | Acetophenone + HCHO + pyrrolidine (Mannich) → cyclohexyl Grignard → hydrolyse |
| Diazepam | 5-Chloro-2-(methylamino)benzophenone + chloroacetyl chloride → ammonia → ring closure |
| Barbital | Diethyl malonate + 2 EtBr/NaOEt → + urea/NaOEt → acidify |
| Chlorpromazine | 2-Chlorophenothiazine + NaNH2 → 1-dimethylamino-3-chloropropane |
| Phenytoin | Benzaldehyde → benzoin → benzil → urea + NaOH (rearrangement) → acidify |
| Ethosuximide | Butanone + ethyl cyanoacetate (Knoevenagel) → HCN → hydrolyse → ammonia (imide) |
| Carbamazepine | Iminostilbene + phosgene → ammonia |
| Halothane | Trichloroethylene + HF (SbF3) → CF3CH2Cl → Br2 → CF3CHBrCl |
| Methohexital | Diethyl malonate + allyl bromide and the pentynyl halide → N-methylurea → NaOH for the salt |
| Ketamine | 2-Chlorobenzonitrile + cyclopentyl Grignard → brominate → methylamine → heat (ring expansion) |
| Fentanyl | N-Phenethyl-4-piperidone + aniline → NaBH4 → propionic anhydride |
| Methadone | Diphenylacetonitrile + dimethylaminochloropropane → EtMgBr → hydrolyse |
| Mefenamic acid | 2-Chlorobenzoic acid + 2,3-dimethylaniline, Cu catalyst (Ullmann) |
| Ibuprofen | Isobutylbenzene + Ac2O/AlCl3 → Darzens with ethyl chloroacetate → aldehyde → acid |

## Pathways worth writing in full

```text
Tyrosine → DOPA → Dopamine → Noradrenaline → Adrenaline
  (tyrosine hydroxylase = rate-limiting; PNMT only in adrenal medulla)
Breakdown: uptake-1, MAO and COMT → VMA in urine

Choline + Acetyl-CoA → Acetylcholine (ChAT)
Acetylcholine → Choline + Acetic acid (AChE: anionic + esteratic site)
```

## One-line contrasts examiners like

| Pair | Difference |
| --- | --- |
| Phase I vs phase II | Phase I adds or exposes a polar group; phase II attaches a polar partner (acetylation and methylation do not raise solubility) |
| Enzyme induction vs inhibition | Induction (phenobarbitone, rifampicin) is slow in and slow out; inhibition (cimetidine, ketoconazole) is immediate |
| AChE vs pseudocholinesterase | True enzyme at the synapse, specific for ACh; plasma enzyme hydrolyses succinylcholine and esters |
| Carbamate vs organophosphate | Carbamoylated enzyme recovers in hours; phosphorylated enzyme does not, and can age |
| Benzodiazepine vs barbiturate | Frequency vs duration of chloride channel opening; benzodiazepine needs GABA, so overdose is safer |
| Tertiary vs quaternary anticholinergic | Atropine (central, oral) vs ipratropium (peripheral, inhaled) |
| Typical vs atypical antipsychotic | D2 blockade with extrapyramidal effects vs added 5-HT2A blockade with fewer movement effects |
| Hydantoin vs succinimide | Aryl substituent → tonic-clonic (phenytoin); small alkyl → absence (ethosuximide) |
| MAC vs blood : gas coefficient | Potency vs speed of induction and recovery |
| Aspirin vs other NSAIDs | Irreversible acetylation of COX vs reversible competition |
| Morphine vs codeine | Free 3-OH vs 3-methyl ether; codeine is a prodrug demethylated by CYP2D6 |

## Numbers and facts worth memorising

| Fact | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Best log P for CNS activity | about 2 |
| Barbiturate C5 substituents, total carbons | about 6–10 |
| Benzodiazepine: essential substituent | electron-withdrawing group at position 7 |
| Phenothiazine side chain | exactly 3 carbons at N10 (2 carbons = antihistamine) |
| Potency order at beta receptors | isoprenaline > adrenaline > noradrenaline |
| Fentanyl potency vs morphine | about 80–100 times |
| Aspirin antiplatelet effect | lasts the platelet lifetime, 7–10 days |
| Final urinary metabolite of catecholamines | vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) |
| Organophosphate poisoning treatment | atropine plus pralidoxime (before ageing) |
| Paracetamol overdose antidote | N-acetylcysteine (replaces glutathione) |

## Named reactions used in this subject

Benzoin condensation and benzilic acid rearrangement (phenytoin) · Knoevenagel (ethosuximide) · Mannich (procyclidine) · Grignard (procyclidine, ketamine, methadone) · Friedel–Crafts acylation (salbutamol, ibuprofen) · Darzens glycidic ester (ibuprofen) · Ullmann condensation (mefenamic acid) · Pinner imino ether (tolazoline) · von Braun demethylation (ipratropium).

# Preparation of 1,3-pyrazole (3,5-dimethylpyrazole)

**Aim:** To prepare 3,5-dimethylpyrazole from acetylacetone and hydrazine hydrate, and to report the yield and melting point.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Hydrazine hydrate is toxic and corrosive: use gloves, goggles and a fume cupboard.

## Principle

A pyrazole is a five-membered ring with two adjacent nitrogen atoms. It is made by a **Knorr pyrazole synthesis**: a 1,3-diketone reacts with hydrazine, each nitrogen attacking one carbonyl group. Two molecules of water are lost and the aromatic ring closes.

```text
CH3-CO-CH2-CO-CH3  +  H2N-NH2   →   3,5-dimethylpyrazole  +  2 H2O
   (acetylacetone)    (hydrazine)        (ring with N-N)
```

The ring is aromatic, weakly basic at N2 and weakly acidic at N1-H, so the product dissolves in both dilute acid and strong alkali.

## Requirements

Acetylacetone (pentane-2,4-dione) 5 ml, hydrazine hydrate (99%) about 2.5 ml, ethanol 15 ml, round-bottomed flask 100 ml, water condenser, water bath, ice bath, Buchner funnel, melting point apparatus.

## Procedure

1. Dissolve 5 ml of acetylacetone in 10 ml of ethanol in a 100 ml round-bottomed flask.
2. Cool the flask in an ice bath and **add the hydrazine hydrate drop by drop** with shaking. The reaction is exothermic.
3. Fit a water condenser and reflux the mixture on a water bath for about 30 minutes.
4. Cool the flask, then pour the contents into about 50 ml of crushed ice and water with stirring.
5. Allow the solid to separate, filter under suction on a Buchner funnel and wash with a little cold water.
6. Recrystallise the crude product from hot water (or aqueous ethanol), dry it between filter papers and then in a desiccator.
7. Record the weight and the melting point, and report the percentage yield.

## Observations and calculation

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Volume (weight) of acetylacetone taken | |
| Theoretical yield (g) | |
| Practical yield (g) | |
| Percentage yield | |
| Melting point found | |
| Reported melting point | about 107–108 °C |

Percentage yield = (practical yield / theoretical yield) × 100.

**Worked example.** 5 ml of acetylacetone (density about 0.97 g/ml) is 4.85 g, that is 0.0485 mol. One mole of diketone gives one mole of 3,5-dimethylpyrazole (molecular weight 96.13), so the theoretical yield is 0.0485 × 96.13 = 4.66 g. If 3.4 g of dry product is obtained, the yield is (3.4/4.66) × 100 = **73%**.

## Result

3,5-Dimethylpyrazole was prepared; weight obtained ___ g, percentage yield ___ %, melting point ___ °C (reported about 107–108 °C).

## Precautions

1. Add hydrazine hydrate slowly and with cooling, since the reaction gives out heat.
2. Keep hydrazine off the skin and avoid breathing the vapour; work in a fume cupboard.
3. Reflux gently; vigorous boiling loses acetylacetone, which is volatile.
4. Dry the crystals completely before taking the melting point, since moisture lowers it.

## Viva questions

1. **What type of reaction is this?** A cyclocondensation (Knorr pyrazole synthesis) between a 1,3-diketone and a hydrazine, with loss of two water molecules.
2. **Why is the product aromatic?** The five-membered ring has six delocalised electrons, counting the lone pair of the N1 nitrogen, so it satisfies Huckel's rule.
3. **Why does the product dissolve in both acid and alkali?** N2 is basic and takes a proton, while the N1-H hydrogen is weakly acidic, so pyrazoles are amphoteric.
4. **Name two drugs containing a pyrazole or pyrazolone ring.** Phenylbutazone and antipyrine (also celecoxib and metamizole).
5. **Why is ethanol used as the solvent?** It dissolves both reactants, boils low enough for a water bath, and the product crystallises when the mixture is poured into water.
6. **What would an unsymmetrical diketone give?** A mixture of two isomeric pyrazoles, since either nitrogen can attack either carbonyl group.

# Preparation of 1,3-oxazole (2,4,5-triphenyloxazole)

**Aim:** To prepare 2,4,5-triphenyloxazole by the fusion of benzoin with benzamide, and to report the yield and melting point.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where they differ. The fusion is carried out at a high temperature, so use a sand bath and a clamp stand, never a naked flame on a glass flask held by hand.

## Principle

An oxazole is a five-membered ring containing one oxygen and one nitrogen at positions 1 and 3. In this **Robinson–Gabriel type synthesis** an alpha-hydroxy ketone (benzoin) reacts with an amide (benzamide). The amide nitrogen attacks the ketone carbonyl and the amide oxygen attacks the carbon bearing the hydroxyl; two molecules of water are then lost and the aromatic ring closes.

```text
C6H5-CO-CH(OH)-C6H5  +  C6H5-CO-NH2
        (benzoin)          (benzamide)
                 │ heat, −2 H2O
      2,4,5-triphenyloxazole   (phenyl groups at C2, C4 and C5)
```

## Requirements

Benzoin 5 g, benzamide 4 g, dry round-bottomed flask 100 ml with air condenser, sand bath, thermometer, ethanol for recrystallisation, Buchner funnel, melting point apparatus.

## Procedure

1. Mix 5 g of benzoin and 4 g of benzamide thoroughly in a dry 100 ml round-bottomed flask and fit an air condenser.
2. Heat the mixture on a sand bath so that it melts and is kept at about 160–180 °C for one and a half to two hours. Swirl occasionally.
3. Allow the melt to cool a little, then pour it while still warm into about 50 ml of cold water with stirring; a solid mass separates.
4. Break up the solid, filter under suction and wash it with warm water to remove unchanged benzamide, which is water soluble.
5. Wash the residue with a little cold alcohol to remove unchanged benzoin.
6. Recrystallise the product from hot ethanol and dry it in a desiccator.
7. Record the weight and the melting point and calculate the percentage yield.

| --- | --- |
| Weight of benzoin taken | |
| Weight of benzamide taken | |
| Theoretical yield (g) | |
| Practical yield (g) | |
| Percentage yield | |
| Melting point found | |
| Reported melting point | about 114–116 °C |

**Worked example.** 5 g of benzoin (molecular weight 212.25) is 0.0236 mol. One mole gives one mole of 2,4,5-triphenyloxazole (molecular weight 297.35), so the theoretical yield is 0.0236 × 297.35 = 7.01 g. If 4.2 g of dry product is obtained, the yield is (4.2/7.01) × 100 = **60%**.

## Result

2,4,5-Triphenyloxazole was prepared; weight obtained ___ g, percentage yield ___ %, melting point ___ °C (reported about 114–116 °C).

## Precautions

1. Both reactants must be dry; moisture reduces the yield because the reaction itself eliminates water.
2. Keep the temperature in the stated range. Below it the reaction is incomplete; well above it the product chars.
3. Pour the hot melt into water carefully and away from the face.
4. Wash with warm water first to remove benzamide; washing with alcohol first dissolves some product.

## Viva questions

1. **Which atoms occupy positions 1 and 3 of the ring?** Oxygen at position 1 and nitrogen at position 3; this is why the ring is called 1,3-oxazole.
2. **What is the role of benzamide?** It supplies the nitrogen and the C2 carbon of the ring and becomes the 2-phenyl substituent.
3. **Why is the product washed with warm water?** Unreacted benzamide dissolves in warm water, while the oxazole does not.
4. **Name a drug containing an oxazole or isoxazole ring.** Cloxacillin and sulphamethoxazole contain an isoxazole ring; oxazole and oxazolidinedione rings appear in trimethadione and in linezolid's oxazolidinone.
5. **How does an oxazole differ from an isoxazole and an imidazole?** In isoxazole the oxygen and nitrogen are adjacent (1,2); in imidazole both heteroatoms are nitrogen at positions 1 and 3.
6. **Is the ring basic?** Only weakly: the nitrogen lone pair is in the plane of the ring and is available, but the electronegative oxygen reduces the basicity well below that of imidazole.

# Preparation of benzimidazole

**Aim:** To prepare benzimidazole from o-phenylenediamine and formic acid, and to report the yield and melting point.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where they differ. o-Phenylenediamine is harmful and stains the skin; formic acid is corrosive.

## Principle

Benzimidazole is a benzene ring fused to an imidazole ring. It is prepared by the **Phillips synthesis**: an aromatic ortho-diamine is condensed with a carboxylic acid. One amino group forms the amide, the second attacks the same carbon, and loss of two water molecules closes the five-membered ring. Formic acid, having one carbon, gives benzimidazole itself; acetic acid would give 2-methylbenzimidazole.

```text
o-C6H4(NH2)2  +  HCOOH   →   benzimidazole  +  2 H2O
```

## Requirements

o-Phenylenediamine 5 g, formic acid (90%) 3 ml, round-bottomed flask 100 ml, water condenser, water bath, 10% ammonia solution, activated charcoal, Buchner funnel, melting point apparatus.

## Procedure

1. Place 5 g of o-phenylenediamine in a 100 ml round-bottomed flask and add 3 ml of 90% formic acid.
2. Fit a water condenser and heat the mixture on a water bath at about 100 °C for two hours.
3. Cool the flask to room temperature.
4. Add 10% ammonia solution slowly with stirring until the mixture is just alkaline to litmus; the crude benzimidazole separates as a solid.
5. Filter under suction, wash the solid with cold water until the washings are neutral, and press it dry.
6. Dissolve the crude solid in about 100 ml of boiling water, add a little activated charcoal, boil for a few minutes and filter hot.
7. Cool the filtrate in ice; colourless needles of benzimidazole separate. Filter, dry and record the weight and melting point.

## Observations and calculation

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Weight of o-phenylenediamine taken | |
| Theoretical yield (g) | |
| Practical yield (g) | |
| Percentage yield | |
| Melting point found | |
| Reported melting point | about 170–172 °C |

**Worked example.** 5 g of o-phenylenediamine (molecular weight 108.14) is 0.0462 mol. One mole gives one mole of benzimidazole (molecular weight 118.14), so the theoretical yield is 0.0462 × 118.14 = 5.46 g. If 3.8 g is obtained, the yield is (3.8/5.46) × 100 = **70%**.

## Result

Benzimidazole was prepared; weight obtained ___ g, percentage yield ___ %, melting point ___ °C (reported about 170–172 °C).

## Precautions

1. Use a slight excess of formic acid, but not a large excess, or the product remains in solution as the formate salt.
2. Neutralise with ammonia slowly and with stirring; the diamine itself dissolves in acid, so precipitation is complete only when the mixture is alkaline.
3. Use charcoal sparingly; too much adsorbs the product and lowers the yield.
4. Dry the crystals fully before the melting point is taken.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the role of ammonia at the end?** It neutralises the excess formic acid and frees benzimidazole from its salt, so the solid separates.
2. **Why is charcoal used?** o-Phenylenediamine oxidises easily and gives coloured impurities; charcoal adsorbs them and gives colourless crystals.
3. **Which drugs contain a benzimidazole ring?** Omeprazole and the other proton pump inhibitors, albendazole and mebendazole, and candesartan and telmisartan.
4. **What product would acetic acid give?** 2-Methylbenzimidazole, since the 2-position carries whatever group the acid supplies.
5. **Is benzimidazole acidic or basic?** Both weakly: the pyridine-type nitrogen is basic and the N-H is weakly acidic, so it is amphoteric and shows tautomerism between the two nitrogens.
6. **Why is water a good recrystallising solvent here?** Benzimidazole is much more soluble in hot water than in cold, so clean needles separate on cooling.

# Preparation of benztriazole

**Aim:** To prepare benztriazole (1H-benzotriazole) from o-phenylenediamine and sodium nitrite in acetic acid, and to report the yield and melting point.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Nitrous acid reactions give off nitrous fumes: work in a fume cupboard and keep the temperature controlled.

## Principle

Sodium nitrite with acetic acid generates **nitrous acid** in situ. One amino group of the ortho-diamine is diazotised, and because the second amino group is held right next to it, the diazonium nitrogen is attacked immediately by that amine. The five-membered ring with three nitrogen atoms closes in the same step, so no separate coupling component is needed.

```text
o-C6H4(NH2)2  +  HNO2   →   benztriazole  +  2 H2O
     (diazotisation followed by immediate intramolecular ring closure)
```

## Requirements

o-Phenylenediamine 5 g, glacial acetic acid 6 ml, sodium nitrite 3.5 g, water, beaker 250 ml, thermometer, ice bath, Buchner funnel, melting point apparatus.

## Procedure

1. Dissolve 5 g of o-phenylenediamine in a mixture of 6 ml of glacial acetic acid and about 15 ml of water in a 250 ml beaker, warming gently if necessary.
2. Cool the solution to about 15 °C in an ice bath.
3. Dissolve 3.5 g of sodium nitrite in 10 ml of water and add this solution **slowly, in small portions**, with constant stirring, keeping the temperature below about 20 °C.
4. After the addition, allow the mixture to stand with stirring; the temperature rises on its own and the colour deepens as the ring closes. Warm on a water bath at about 60–70 °C for 15 minutes to complete the reaction.
5. Cool the mixture thoroughly in ice; benztriazole separates as a crystalline solid.
6. Filter under suction and wash with a little cold water.
7. Recrystallise from hot water (or aqueous ethanol), dry the crystals and record the weight and melting point.

## Observations and calculation

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Weight of o-phenylenediamine taken | |
| Theoretical yield (g) | |
| Practical yield (g) | |
| Percentage yield | |
| Melting point found | |
| Reported melting point | about 98–100 °C |

**Worked example.** 5 g of o-phenylenediamine (molecular weight 108.14) is 0.0462 mol. One mole gives one mole of benztriazole (molecular weight 119.12), so the theoretical yield is 0.0462 × 119.12 = 5.50 g. If 3.6 g is obtained, the yield is (3.6/5.50) × 100 = **65%**.

## Result

Benztriazole was prepared; weight obtained ___ g, percentage yield ___ %, melting point ___ °C (reported about 98–100 °C).

## Precautions

1. Add the nitrite solution slowly and keep the mixture cool during the addition, or the diazonium intermediate decomposes and the yield falls.
2. Use a fume cupboard; nitrous fumes are irritant.
3. Do not use mineral acid in place of acetic acid in this preparation; the mild acid favours the internal ring closure.
4. Cool well before filtering, as benztriazole is appreciably soluble in warm water.

## Viva questions

1. **How is nitrous acid produced here?** Sodium nitrite reacts with acetic acid in the flask, so the unstable acid is formed just as it is needed.
2. **Why is no coupling component added?** The second amino group of the same molecule attacks the diazonium group, giving an intramolecular ring closure.
3. **How many nitrogen atoms are in the triazole ring, and where?** Three, at positions 1, 2 and 3 of the five-membered ring fused to benzene.
4. **Why is the temperature kept low during addition?** Diazonium salts decompose above about 20 °C, giving phenols and nitrogen gas.
5. **Give one use of benztriazole.** It is a corrosion inhibitor for copper and a useful synthetic intermediate; the triazole ring itself appears in drugs such as fluconazole and in benzotriazole-based coupling reagents.
6. **How would you confirm the product?** By its sharp melting point near 99 °C and by a mixed melting point with an authentic sample.

# Preparation of 2,3-diphenylquinoxaline

**Aim:** To prepare 2,3-diphenylquinoxaline from benzil and o-phenylenediamine, and to report the yield and melting point.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where they differ.

## Principle

A quinoxaline is a benzene ring fused to a pyrazine ring. It is formed when an aromatic **ortho-diamine** condenses with a **1,2-diketone**: each amino group attacks one carbonyl carbon, two molecules of water are eliminated and the six-membered ring with two nitrogens closes. The reaction is fast, clean and almost quantitative, which is why it is also used as a test for 1,2-diketones.

```text
C6H5-CO-CO-C6H5  +  o-C6H4(NH2)2   →   2,3-diphenylquinoxaline  +  2 H2O
     (benzil)        (o-phenylenediamine)
```

## Requirements

Benzil 4 g, o-phenylenediamine 2.2 g, ethanol 40 ml, round-bottomed flask 100 ml, water condenser, water bath, Buchner funnel, melting point apparatus.

## Procedure

1. Dissolve 4 g of benzil in about 25 ml of warm ethanol in a 100 ml round-bottomed flask.
2. Dissolve 2.2 g of o-phenylenediamine in 15 ml of ethanol and add it to the flask.
3. Fit a water condenser and reflux the mixture on a water bath for about 30 minutes. The solution darkens as the reaction proceeds.
4. Cool the flask in ice; pale yellow crystals separate. If they do not, add a little water drop by drop to start crystallisation.
5. Filter under suction and wash with a little cold ethanol.
6. Recrystallise from hot ethanol, dry the crystals and record the weight and melting point.

## Observations and calculation

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Weight of benzil taken | |
| Weight of o-phenylenediamine taken | |
| Theoretical yield (g) | |
| Practical yield (g) | |
| Percentage yield | |
| Melting point found | |
| Reported melting point | about 125–126 °C |

**Worked example.** 4 g of benzil (molecular weight 210.23) is 0.0190 mol; 2.2 g of o-phenylenediamine (molecular weight 108.14) is 0.0203 mol, so benzil is the limiting reactant. One mole gives one mole of 2,3-diphenylquinoxaline (molecular weight 282.34), so the theoretical yield is 0.0190 × 282.34 = 5.37 g. If 4.3 g is obtained, the yield is (4.3/5.37) × 100 = **80%**.

## Result

2,3-Diphenylquinoxaline was prepared; weight obtained ___ g, percentage yield ___ %, melting point ___ °C (reported about 125–126 °C).

## Precautions

1. Use a very slight excess of the diamine only; a large excess colours the product.
2. Reflux gently and keep the condenser running, since ethanol is volatile and inflammable. Never heat it over a flame.
3. Cool well before filtering so that crystallisation is complete.
4. Dry the crystals before taking the melting point.

## Viva questions

1. **What type of reaction is this?** A condensation (cyclocondensation) between a 1,2-diketone and an ortho-diamine, with loss of two water molecules.
2. **Why is the reaction used as a test for 1,2-diketones?** Only a diketone with the two carbonyls adjacent can form the six-membered ring, and the product is a well-defined crystalline solid.
3. **Name the ring system formed.** Quinoxaline, that is benzopyrazine: a benzene ring fused to a pyrazine ring with nitrogen at positions 1 and 4.
4. **How is benzil obtained?** By oxidising benzoin with concentrated nitric acid or with copper(II) sulphate in pyridine.
5. **Mention a medicinal use of the quinoxaline ring.** Quinoxaline 1,4-dioxides have antibacterial activity, and the ring appears in the antiviral and anticancer field as well as in dyes.
6. **Why is ethanol chosen as the solvent?** Both reactants dissolve in it when warm, and the product is much less soluble when cold, so it crystallises directly.

# Preparation of benzocaine

**Aim:** To prepare benzocaine (ethyl p-aminobenzoate) from p-aminobenzoic acid and ethanol, and to report the yield and melting point.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Concentrated sulphuric acid is highly corrosive: add it slowly to the cooled alcohol, never the reverse.

## Principle

Benzocaine is the ethyl ester of p-aminobenzoic acid and is a local anaesthetic of the ester type. It is prepared by **Fischer esterification**: the carboxylic acid is heated with an excess of ethanol in the presence of a catalytic amount of concentrated sulphuric acid. The reaction is reversible, so a large excess of alcohol is used to drive it forward.

```text
H2N-C6H4-COOH  +  C2H5OH   ⇌   H2N-C6H4-COOC2H5  +  H2O
   (p-aminobenzoic acid)            (benzocaine)
```

During the reaction the amino group is protonated by the acid and the product stays in solution as the sulphate salt; neutralisation with sodium carbonate at the end liberates the free base, which separates as a solid.

## Requirements

p-Aminobenzoic acid 5 g, absolute ethanol 50 ml, concentrated sulphuric acid 5 ml, 10% sodium carbonate solution, round-bottomed flask 250 ml, water condenser, water bath, litmus paper, Buchner funnel, melting point apparatus.

## Procedure

1. Place 5 g of p-aminobenzoic acid and 50 ml of absolute ethanol in a 250 ml round-bottomed flask and swirl to dissolve.
2. Cool the flask in cold water and add 5 ml of concentrated sulphuric acid slowly down the side with swirling. A precipitate may appear and then dissolve on heating.
3. Fit a water condenser and reflux the mixture on a water bath for about one and a half to two hours.
4. Cool the mixture and distil off most of the excess ethanol on a water bath (or pour the mixture into about 100 ml of water).
5. Add 10% sodium carbonate solution **slowly** with stirring until the mixture is just alkaline to litmus; carbon dioxide is evolved and benzocaine separates as a white solid.
6. Filter under suction, wash with cold water until free of alkali and press dry.
7. Recrystallise from aqueous ethanol (dissolve in the least hot ethanol, then add hot water until turbid and cool). Dry and record the weight and melting point.

## Observations and calculation

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Weight of p-aminobenzoic acid taken | |
| Theoretical yield (g) | |
| Practical yield (g) | |
| Percentage yield | |
| Melting point found | |
| Reported melting point | about 88–90 °C |

**Worked example.** 5 g of p-aminobenzoic acid (molecular weight 137.14) is 0.0365 mol. One mole gives one mole of benzocaine (molecular weight 165.19), so the theoretical yield is 0.0365 × 165.19 = 6.03 g. If 4.2 g is obtained, the yield is (4.2/6.03) × 100 = **70%**.

## Result

Benzocaine was prepared; weight obtained ___ g, percentage yield ___ %, melting point ___ °C (reported about 88–90 °C).

## Precautions

1. Add sulphuric acid slowly to the cooled alcoholic solution, never water or alkali to the acid directly.
2. Use absolute (dry) ethanol; water shifts the equilibrium back towards the acid.
3. Neutralise slowly, as carbon dioxide froths; stop as soon as the mixture is just alkaline, since excess alkali can hydrolyse the ester.
4. Wash the product free of alkali and dry it well before taking the melting point.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the role of sulphuric acid?** It is a catalyst that protonates the carbonyl oxygen and makes the carbon more electrophilic; it also removes water, helping the equilibrium.
2. **Why is excess ethanol used?** The esterification is reversible, so an excess of one reactant drives the equilibrium towards the ester (Le Chatelier's principle).
3. **Why does the product dissolve during the reaction and separate on neutralisation?** In acid the amino group is protonated and the salt is water soluble; sodium carbonate frees the base, which is insoluble.
4. **Why is sodium carbonate used instead of sodium hydroxide?** It is mild enough to neutralise the mineral acid without hydrolysing the ester back to the acid.
5. **To which class of local anaesthetics does benzocaine belong, and what is its main use?** The ester class; it is used for surface anaesthesia of skin and mucous membranes, in lozenges and in ointments.
6. **Why is benzocaine only a surface anaesthetic?** It has no basic side-chain nitrogen, so it is very poorly water soluble and cannot be given by injection like procaine or lignocaine.

# Preparation of phenytoin

**Aim:** To prepare phenytoin (5,5-diphenylhydantoin) from benzil and urea, and to report the yield and melting point.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Sodium hydroxide solution is corrosive; wear goggles.

## Principle

Benzil is a 1,2-diketone. In hot alcoholic alkali, one nitrogen of **urea** attacks a carbonyl carbon; the alkoxide then drives a **benzilic acid type rearrangement**, in which a phenyl group migrates so that both phenyl groups end up on the same carbon. The second nitrogen closes the five-membered hydantoin ring. The product first forms as the water-soluble sodium salt, and the free drug is precipitated by acid.

```text
C6H5-CO-CO-C6H5  +  H2N-CO-NH2   --NaOH/ethanol-->   sodium phenytoin
                                      --HCl-->       phenytoin (5,5-diphenylhydantoin)
```

If benzil is not available it is prepared first from benzoin by oxidation with concentrated nitric acid, benzoin itself being made from benzaldehyde by the benzoin condensation.

## Requirements

Benzil 4 g, urea 1.5 g, 30% sodium hydroxide solution 10 ml, ethanol (95%) 30 ml, dilute hydrochloric acid, activated charcoal, round-bottomed flask 250 ml, water condenser, water bath, Buchner funnel, melting point apparatus.

## Procedure

1. Place 4 g of benzil, 1.5 g of urea and 30 ml of ethanol in a 250 ml round-bottomed flask.
2. Add 10 ml of 30% sodium hydroxide solution, fit a water condenser and reflux the mixture on a water bath for about two hours.
3. Pour the hot mixture into about 100 ml of water, stir well and let it stand for 15 minutes. A small amount of insoluble by-product may appear.
4. Filter off the insoluble material; the filtrate contains the sodium salt of phenytoin.
5. Treat the filtrate with a little activated charcoal, boil and filter hot.
6. Cool the clear filtrate and acidify it carefully with dilute hydrochloric acid until just acidic to litmus. Phenytoin separates as a white solid.
7. Filter under suction, wash with cold water until the washings are neutral, dry, and recrystallise from ethanol.
8. Record the weight and the melting point and calculate the percentage yield.

## Observations and calculation

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Weight of benzil taken | |
| Weight of urea taken | |
| Theoretical yield (g) | |
| Practical yield (g) | |
| Percentage yield | |
| Melting point found | |
| Reported melting point | about 295–298 °C |

**Worked example.** 4 g of benzil (molecular weight 210.23) is 0.0190 mol. One mole gives one mole of phenytoin (molecular weight 252.27), so the theoretical yield is 0.0190 × 252.27 = 4.79 g. If 3.1 g is obtained, the yield is (3.1/4.79) × 100 = **65%**.

## Result

Phenytoin was prepared; weight obtained ___ g, percentage yield ___ %, melting point ___ °C (reported about 295–298 °C).

## Precautions

1. Reflux long enough; a short reaction leaves unchanged benzil, which shows as yellow colour in the product.
2. Filter off the insoluble by-product before acidifying, or it contaminates the phenytoin.
3. Acidify slowly and only to the point where the solution is just acidic; a large excess of acid is wasteful and can make the product sticky.
4. Use a high-range melting point apparatus, since phenytoin melts near 300 °C.

## Viva questions

1. **Which rearrangement occurs in this preparation?** A benzilic acid type rearrangement, in which a phenyl group migrates from one carbonyl carbon to the next, so that both phenyls sit on C5 of the hydantoin ring.
2. **Why does the product first stay in solution?** The imide hydrogen is weakly acidic, so in alkali the drug exists as its soluble sodium salt.
3. **What is the role of urea?** It supplies the two nitrogen atoms and the C2 carbonyl of the hydantoin ring.
4. **How is benzil prepared?** By oxidation of benzoin with concentrated nitric acid, or with copper(II) sulphate in pyridine.
5. **What is the therapeutic use of phenytoin?** It is an anticonvulsant for generalised tonic-clonic and partial seizures and for status epilepticus; it also has antiarrhythmic use.
6. **Why is the injection given as the sodium salt?** The free acid is practically insoluble in water; the sodium salt dissolves, but the solution is strongly alkaline and must be given slowly.

# Preparation of phenothiazine

**Aim:** To prepare phenothiazine by the fusion of diphenylamine with sulphur, and to report the yield and melting point.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Hydrogen sulphide is evolved: the whole fusion must be done in a fume cupboard.

## Principle

Phenothiazine is a tricyclic system in which two benzene rings are joined by a sulphur atom and a nitrogen atom. It is prepared by heating **diphenylamine with sulphur**, using a trace of **iodine** as catalyst. Sulphur enters both positions ortho to the nitrogen bridge and the central six-membered ring closes, with hydrogen sulphide being evolved.

```text
(C6H5)2NH  +  2 S   --I2, heat-->   phenothiazine  +  H2S
```

The ring formed here is the nucleus of chlorpromazine and the other phenothiazine antipsychotics; the drug is made by alkylating the ring nitrogen of the corresponding 2-chloro compound.

## Requirements

Diphenylamine 10 g, sulphur (powdered) 4 g, iodine 0.1 g, round-bottomed flask 100 ml with air condenser, sand bath or heating mantle, thermometer, toluene or ethanol for recrystallisation, Buchner funnel, melting point apparatus.

## Procedure

1. Mix 10 g of diphenylamine, 4 g of powdered sulphur and about 0.1 g of iodine in a dry 100 ml round-bottomed flask and fit an air condenser.
2. Heat the mixture in a fume cupboard on a sand bath, raising the temperature slowly to about 180 °C. Hydrogen sulphide is given off; lead acetate paper held at the mouth of the condenser turns black.
3. Continue heating at this temperature until the evolution of hydrogen sulphide stops, usually about two hours. The melt turns dark.
4. Allow the melt to cool until it is still warm, then add about 40 ml of toluene and warm to dissolve the product.
5. Filter the hot solution to remove unchanged sulphur and tarry matter.
6. Cool the filtrate in ice; greenish-yellow crystals of phenothiazine separate. Filter under suction and wash with a little cold solvent.
7. Recrystallise from toluene (or ethanol), dry in a desiccator and record the weight and melting point.

## Observations and calculation

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Weight of diphenylamine taken | |
| Theoretical yield (g) | |
| Practical yield (g) | |
| Percentage yield | |
| Melting point found | |
| Reported melting point | about 185 °C |

**Worked example.** 10 g of diphenylamine (molecular weight 169.22) is 0.0591 mol. One mole gives one mole of phenothiazine (molecular weight 199.27), so the theoretical yield is 0.0591 × 199.27 = 11.78 g. If 7.1 g of dry product is obtained, the yield is (7.1/11.78) × 100 = **60%**.

## Result

Phenothiazine was prepared; weight obtained ___ g, percentage yield ___ %, melting point ___ °C (reported about 185 °C).

## Precautions

1. Carry out the fusion only in a fume cupboard; hydrogen sulphide is toxic and has a foul smell.
2. Raise the temperature gradually, since frothing occurs when the gas is evolved.
3. Do not let the melt solidify completely before adding the solvent, or it becomes very difficult to remove from the flask.
4. Filter the hot solution to remove unchanged sulphur, which would otherwise contaminate the crystals.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the role of iodine?** It is the catalyst; it helps sulphur attack the aromatic rings, so the reaction goes at a lower temperature and in a shorter time.
2. **How do you know the reaction is proceeding?** Hydrogen sulphide is evolved, which blackens lead acetate paper; the end of gas evolution signals completion.
3. **Which positions of diphenylamine are attacked?** The two positions ortho to the nitrogen, so that a six-membered central ring containing S and N is formed.
4. **Name three drugs built on this nucleus.** Chlorpromazine, trifluoperazine and thioridazine (promethazine is the antihistaminic member).
5. **Which position of the ring carries the substituent in antipsychotics, and why?** Position 2, with an electron-withdrawing group such as Cl or CF3; it increases potency and makes the molecule asymmetric.
6. **Why does the solid darken on storage?** Phenothiazine oxidises in air and light to coloured sulphoxide and other products, so it is stored in a well-closed, light-resistant container.

# Preparation of a barbiturate (barbituric acid)

**Aim:** To prepare barbituric acid by condensing diethyl malonate with urea in the presence of sodium ethoxide, and to report the yield and melting point.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your own lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Sodium metal reacts violently with water: cut it under kerosene, handle with dry forceps and never let it touch water or wet glassware.

## Principle

A barbiturate is a cyclic ureide formed from a **malonic ester and urea**. Sodium ethoxide, made from sodium and absolute alcohol, removes a proton and makes urea nucleophilic; each nitrogen then attacks one ester group, two molecules of ethanol are eliminated and the six-membered ring closes. The product separates first as its sodium salt and is set free by acid.

```text
CH2(COOC2H5)2  +  H2N-CO-NH2   --NaOC2H5-->   barbituric acid  +  2 C2H5OH
```

The hypnotic barbiturates are made by the same route after both hydrogens at C5 have been replaced: diethyl **diethyl**malonate with urea gives barbital, and diethyl ethylphenylmalonate gives phenobarbital. Barbituric acid itself is **not** a hypnotic, because C5 carries no substituents.

## Requirements

Sodium metal 1.5 g, absolute ethanol 40 ml, diethyl malonate 6 ml, dry urea 4 g, concentrated hydrochloric acid, round-bottomed flask 250 ml with a calcium chloride guard tube, water bath, Buchner funnel, melting point apparatus.

## Procedure

1. Dissolve 1.5 g of clean, dry sodium metal in 40 ml of absolute ethanol in a dry 250 ml round-bottomed flask fitted with a condenser and a calcium chloride guard tube. Allow the sodium to react completely.
2. To the warm sodium ethoxide solution add 6 ml of diethyl malonate and swirl.
3. Add 4 g of dry urea dissolved in the least quantity of warm absolute alcohol.
4. Reflux the mixture on a water bath for about two hours, protecting it from moisture. A white solid (the sodium salt) separates.
5. Cool the mixture, add about 50 ml of warm water to dissolve the sodium salt.
6. Acidify the clear solution with concentrated hydrochloric acid until just acidic to litmus and cool in ice. Barbituric acid crystallises out.
7. Filter under suction, wash with a little cold water, dry and recrystallise from hot water.
8. Record the weight and melting point and calculate the percentage yield.

## Observations and calculation

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Volume (weight) of diethyl malonate taken | |
| Weight of urea taken | |
| Theoretical yield (g) | |
| Practical yield (g) | |
| Percentage yield | |
| Melting behaviour | melts above about 245 °C with decomposition |

**Worked example.** 6 ml of diethyl malonate (density about 1.055 g/ml) is 6.33 g, that is 0.0395 mol (molecular weight 160.17). One mole gives one mole of barbituric acid (molecular weight 128.09), so the theoretical yield is 0.0395 × 128.09 = 5.06 g. If 3.0 g is obtained, the yield is (3.0/5.06) × 100 = **59%**.

## Result

Barbituric acid was prepared; weight obtained ___ g, percentage yield ___ %, melting behaviour ___ (reported to melt above about 245 °C with decomposition).

## Precautions

1. Everything must be dry: absolute alcohol, dry urea and dry glassware, since water destroys sodium ethoxide.
2. Add sodium in small pieces and let each dissolve before adding the next; keep the flask protected from moisture with a guard tube.
3. Do not let unreacted sodium remain at the end of the experiment; destroy any residue carefully with alcohol, never with water.
4. Acidify only to the point where the solution is just acidic, and cool well before filtering.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is sodium ethoxide used?** It is a strong enough base to generate the nucleophile and to keep the reaction free of water; it also drives off ethanol as the ring closes.
2. **Why is barbituric acid itself inactive as a hypnotic?** Both hydrogens at C5 are free; activity requires a 5,5-disubstituted compound with about six to ten carbon atoms in the two substituents.
3. **How would you prepare barbital by this route?** Alkylate diethyl malonate twice with ethyl bromide and sodium ethoxide, then condense the diethyl diethylmalonate with urea.
4. **Why are barbiturates acidic?** The imide hydrogen between the two carbonyl groups is weakly acidic, and the resulting anion is stabilised by resonance; the sodium salts are therefore water soluble.
5. **What happens to the duration of action if the C2 oxygen is replaced by sulphur?** The compound becomes far more lipid soluble and ultra-short acting, as with thiopental.
6. **Which simple test identifies a barbiturate?** It gives a violet colour with cobalt nitrate in an alkaline medium, and it is soluble in sodium hydroxide, being reprecipitated by acid.

# Assay of chlorpromazine hydrochloride

**Aim:** To determine the percentage purity of chlorpromazine hydrochloride by non-aqueous titration.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your own lab manual, the current Indian Pharmacopoeia monograph and your teacher where they differ. Perchloric acid, glacial acetic acid and acetic anhydride are corrosive, and mercuric acetate is highly toxic: handle in a fume cupboard and collect mercury waste separately.

## Principle

Chlorpromazine hydrochloride is the salt of a weak base (the aliphatic tertiary amine of the side chain; the ring nitrogen is not appreciably basic) with a strong acid. In water this base is too weak to be titrated sharply. In **glacial acetic acid**, which is a weakly basic solvent for this purpose, the base is strengthened and can be titrated with **perchloric acid**, the strongest acid in that medium.

The chloride of the salt would otherwise behave as a strong acid and prevent titration, so **mercuric acetate** is added; it ties up the chloride as undissociated mercuric chloride and liberates an equivalent amount of acetate, which is titratable.

```text
Drug.HCl + Hg(CH3COO)2  →  Drug.CH3COOH  +  HgCl2 (undissociated)
Drug (base) + HClO4     →  Drug.HClO4
```

**Each ml of 0.1 M perchloric acid is equivalent to 35.53 mg of chlorpromazine hydrochloride** (molecular weight 355.33, one basic centre titrated).

## Requirements

Chlorpromazine hydrochloride sample, glacial acetic acid, 5% w/v mercuric acetate in glacial acetic acid, 0.1 M perchloric acid (standardised against potassium hydrogen phthalate), crystal violet indicator (0.5% in glacial acetic acid) or a potentiometric assembly, conical flask with stopper, burette, analytical balance.

## Procedure

1. Weigh accurately about 0.5 g of the sample and transfer it to a dry conical flask.
2. Dissolve it in about 50 ml of glacial acetic acid, warming gently if needed, and cool.
3. Add 10 ml of mercuric acetate solution and 2 to 3 drops of crystal violet indicator.
4. Titrate with 0.1 M perchloric acid until the violet colour changes to blue-green (or determine the end point potentiometrically).
5. Carry out a **blank titration** with the same volumes of all reagents but no sample, and subtract the blank reading.
6. Repeat until two concordant readings are obtained.

## Observations and calculation

| Reading | Weight of sample (g) | Burette initial (ml) | Burette final (ml) | Volume used (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | | | | |
| 2 | | | | |
| Blank | — | | | |

Corrected volume V = (titre − blank), in ml.

Percentage purity = (V × molarity factor × 35.53 × 100) / (weight of sample in mg), where the molarity factor is (actual molarity of perchloric acid / 0.1).

**Worked example.** Sample 0.5120 g (512.0 mg); titre 14.6 ml; blank 0.2 ml; perchloric acid exactly 0.1 M. Corrected volume = 14.4 ml. Chlorpromazine hydrochloride found = 14.4 × 35.53 = 511.6 mg. Percentage purity = (511.6/512.0) × 100 = **99.9%**.

## Result

The sample of chlorpromazine hydrochloride contains ___ % w/w of C17H19ClN2S,HCl (the pharmacopoeial limit is given in the current monograph, normally not less than 98.5% and not more than 101.0% on the dried basis).

## Precautions

1. All glassware and reagents must be dry; water in the system blunts the end point because it is a stronger base than the drug.
2. Standardise the perchloric acid on the day of use and apply a temperature correction if the laboratory temperature differs much from that of standardisation, since glacial acetic acid expands markedly.
3. Always run a blank; mercuric acetate solution itself consumes a little titrant.
4. Dispose of mercury-containing waste in the labelled container, never down the sink.
5. Protect the drug from light; phenothiazines oxidise to pink or violet products in light and air.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is the titration carried out in a non-aqueous medium?** The drug is a weak base whose salt gives no sharp end point in water; glacial acetic acid enhances its basic strength so a sharp titration is possible.
2. **What is the role of mercuric acetate?** It removes the chloride ion as undissociated mercuric chloride, replacing a strong acid by titratable acetate.
3. **Why is crystal violet suitable?** It changes colour in the acidic non-aqueous range, giving a violet to blue-green transition at the end point.
4. **Why is a blank required?** The reagents, especially mercuric acetate and the solvent, consume a small volume of titrant that must be subtracted.
5. **Name another assay method for chlorpromazine.** Ultraviolet spectrophotometry and cerimetric titration have been used; high performance liquid chromatography is used for related substances.
6. **Why must the sample be protected from light?** The phenothiazine ring oxidises to sulphoxide and coloured products, which would make the assay and the colour of the solution unreliable.

# Assay of phenobarbitone

**Aim:** To determine the percentage purity of phenobarbitone by non-aqueous titration with sodium methoxide.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your own lab manual, the current Indian Pharmacopoeia monograph and your teacher where they differ. Dimethylformamide and methanol are harmful by inhalation; sodium methoxide is corrosive. Work in a fume cupboard.

## Principle

Phenobarbitone is a very weak acid: the hydrogen of the imide group (-CO-NH-CO-) between the two carbonyl groups can be removed because the resulting anion is stabilised by resonance. The acid is far too weak for a sharp titration in water, so a **basic solvent, dimethylformamide**, is used. It accepts the proton readily and so strengthens the acid, allowing titration with the strong base **sodium methoxide** in a methanol–toluene mixture.

```text
Phenobarbitone (imide H)  +  CH3ONa   →   sodium phenobarbitone  +  CH3OH
```

**Each ml of 0.1 M sodium methoxide is equivalent to 23.22 mg of phenobarbitone** (molecular weight 232.24, one acidic hydrogen titrated).

## Requirements

Phenobarbitone sample, dimethylformamide (neutralised), 0.1 M sodium methoxide (standardised against benzoic acid), thymol blue indicator (0.3% in methanol) or a potentiometric assembly, nitrogen cylinder with delivery tube, conical flask with a two-holed stopper, burette protected with a guard tube, analytical balance.

## Procedure

1. Weigh accurately about 0.2 g of phenobarbitone and dissolve it in about 25 ml of dimethylformamide in a dry conical flask.
2. Pass a slow stream of **nitrogen** through the flask throughout the titration, to keep out carbon dioxide and moisture.
3. Add 2 to 3 drops of thymol blue indicator; the solution is yellow.
4. Titrate with 0.1 M sodium methoxide from a burette fitted with a guard tube until the colour changes to **blue**.
5. Perform a blank titration on the same volume of dimethylformamide and subtract it.
6. Repeat for concordant readings.

## Observations and calculation

| Reading | Weight of sample (g) | Burette initial (ml) | Burette final (ml) | Volume used (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | | | | |
| 2 | | | | |
| Blank | — | | | |

Corrected volume V = (titre − blank), in ml.

Percentage purity = (V × molarity factor × 23.22 × 100) / (weight of sample in mg).

**Worked example.** Sample 0.2015 g (201.5 mg); titre 9.0 ml; blank 0.3 ml; titrant exactly 0.1 M. Corrected volume = 8.7 ml. Phenobarbitone found = 8.7 × 23.22 = 202.0 mg. Percentage purity = (202.0/201.5) × 100 = **100.2%**.

## Result

The sample of phenobarbitone contains ___ % w/w of C12H12N2O3 (the pharmacopoeial limit is given in the current monograph, normally not less than 99.0% and not more than 101.0% on the dried basis).

## Precautions

1. Keep carbon dioxide out: it is an acid in this medium and would be titrated along with the drug, so the nitrogen stream and the guard tube are essential.
2. Use neutralised, water-free dimethylformamide and standardise the titrant on the day of use, as sodium methoxide absorbs carbon dioxide on storage.
3. Always subtract the blank.
4. Add the indicator after dissolving the sample, and judge the first permanent blue tint as the end point.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is phenobarbitone acidic?** The imide hydrogen between the two carbonyl groups is removed easily because the resulting anion is resonance stabilised.
2. **Why is dimethylformamide used?** It is a basic (protophilic) solvent that accepts the proton and so levels up the apparent strength of a very weak acid, giving a sharp end point.
3. **Why pass nitrogen through the flask?** To exclude atmospheric carbon dioxide and moisture, both of which would consume titrant and blur the end point.
4. **What indicator is used and what is the colour change?** Thymol blue, which changes from yellow to blue.
5. **Name an alternative assay for a barbiturate.** Argentimetric titration with silver nitrate in an alkaline medium, or an ultraviolet spectrophotometric method in alkaline borate buffer.
6. **Why is the sodium salt of phenobarbitone used for injection?** The free acid is practically insoluble in water, while the sodium salt dissolves readily, though the solution is alkaline and hydrolyses on storage.

# Assay of atropine sulphate

**Aim:** To determine the percentage purity of atropine sulphate by non-aqueous titration with perchloric acid.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your own lab manual, the current Indian Pharmacopoeia monograph and your teacher where they differ. Atropine is a potent drug: do not taste or handle it carelessly. Perchloric acid, acetic anhydride and glacial acetic acid are corrosive.

## Principle

Atropine sulphate is the sulphate salt of a weak organic base; its molecule contains **two atropine units** joined to one molecule of sulphuric acid. In water the base is too weak to be titrated sharply. In **anhydrous (glacial) acetic acid** the basicity is enhanced and the drug can be titrated with **0.1 M perchloric acid** using crystal violet as indicator.

Sulphuric acid behaves as a weak acid in glacial acetic acid and does not interfere, so no mercuric acetate is required here (unlike a hydrochloride). Both tertiary nitrogen atoms of the two atropine molecules take up one proton each.

**Each ml of 0.1 M perchloric acid is equivalent to 67.68 mg of anhydrous atropine sulphate**, that is one-tenth of a millimole of the salt (molecular weight 676.8). In glacial acetic acid the two atropine units are already protonated; what the perchloric acid titrates is the sulphate ion, which takes up one proton to become hydrogen sulphate (HSO4⁻). So one mole of perchloric acid corresponds to one mole of the salt. Check the factor against the current Indian Pharmacopoeia monograph.

## Requirements

Atropine sulphate sample, anhydrous (glacial) acetic acid, acetic anhydride, 0.1 M perchloric acid (standardised against potassium hydrogen phthalate), crystal violet indicator, dry conical flask, burette with guard tube, analytical balance, drying oven.

## Procedure

1. Dry the sample to constant weight as directed in the monograph, since the official salt is a monohydrate and the assay is reported on the dried basis.
2. Weigh accurately about 0.5 g of the dried sample into a dry conical flask.
3. Dissolve it in about 20 ml of anhydrous acetic acid, warming gently if necessary; cool. Where directed, add a few ml of acetic anhydride to remove traces of water.
4. Add 2 to 3 drops of crystal violet indicator.
5. Titrate with 0.1 M perchloric acid until the violet colour changes to **blue-green**, or find the end point potentiometrically.
6. Carry out a blank titration and subtract it.
7. Repeat for concordant readings.

## Observations and calculation

| Reading | Weight of sample (g) | Burette initial (ml) | Burette final (ml) | Volume used (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | | | | |
| 2 | | | | |
| Blank | — | | | |

Corrected volume V = (titre − blank), in ml.

Percentage purity = (V × molarity factor × 67.68 × 100) / (weight of dried sample in mg).

**Worked example.** Dried sample 0.5050 g (505.0 mg); titre 7.65 ml; blank 0.20 ml; acid exactly 0.1 M. Corrected volume = 7.45 ml. Atropine sulphate found = 7.45 × 67.68 = 504.2 mg. Percentage purity = (504.2/505.0) × 100 = **99.8%**.

## Result

The sample of atropine sulphate contains ___ % w/w of (C17H23NO3)2,H2SO4 calculated on the dried basis (the limit is given in the current monograph, normally not less than 98.5%).

## Precautions

1. All glassware and solvents must be dry; water weakens the end point because it competes as a base.
2. Standardise the perchloric acid on the day of use and correct for temperature, as glacial acetic acid has a large coefficient of expansion.
3. Dry the sample as directed before weighing, otherwise the water of crystallisation gives a low result.
4. Run a blank and subtract it.
5. Handle the alkaloid with care; it is toxic in small quantities.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is mercuric acetate not needed here?** The counter-ion is sulphate, and sulphuric acid is only weakly acidic in glacial acetic acid, so it does not interfere; a hydrochloride would need mercuric acetate.
2. **Why is the equivalence 67.68 mg (one whole mole of salt per mole of acid) and not half of it?** The atropine units are already protonated in the salt. In glacial acetic acid the acid titrates the sulphate ion, which takes only one proton (SO4²⁻ → HSO4⁻), so one mole of perchloric acid corresponds to one mole of atropine sulphate.
3. **What chemical type is atropine?** A tropane alkaloid, the ester of tropic acid with tropine; it is the racemic form of hyoscyamine.
4. **Give two therapeutic uses of atropine sulphate.** As a mydriatic and cycloplegic in the eye, as an antispasmodic and drying agent before anaesthesia, and as an antidote in organophosphate poisoning and severe bradycardia.
5. **Which test identifies atropine chemically?** The Vitali–Morin test: the alkaloid is treated with fuming nitric acid, evaporated, and the residue with alcoholic potassium hydroxide gives a violet colour.
6. **Why is the assay reported on the dried basis?** The official substance is a hydrate, and the water content varies, so the result is corrected to the dried material for comparability.

# Assay of ibuprofen

**Aim:** To determine the percentage purity of ibuprofen by direct acid–base titration in alcohol.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your own lab manual, the current Indian Pharmacopoeia monograph and your teacher where they differ.

## Principle

Ibuprofen, 2-(4-isobutylphenyl)propanoic acid, is a carboxylic acid that is practically insoluble in water but dissolves freely in alcohol. It is therefore dissolved in **neutralised ethanol** and titrated directly with standard **sodium hydroxide** using phenolphthalein, the alcohol serving only as the solvent.

```text
R-COOH  +  NaOH   →   R-COONa  +  H2O
```

**Each ml of 0.1 M sodium hydroxide is equivalent to 20.63 mg of ibuprofen** (molecular weight 206.28, one carboxyl group).

## Requirements

Ibuprofen sample, ethanol (95%), 0.1 M sodium hydroxide (standardised against potassium hydrogen phthalate), phenolphthalein solution, conical flask 250 ml, burette, analytical balance.

## Procedure

1. Take about 50 ml of ethanol in a conical flask, add a few drops of phenolphthalein and **neutralise it** by adding 0.1 M sodium hydroxide drop by drop until a faint permanent pink appears. This removes any acidity of the solvent.
2. Weigh accurately about 0.5 g of ibuprofen and dissolve it in the neutralised alcohol; the pink colour disappears.
3. Titrate with 0.1 M sodium hydroxide, swirling constantly, until a pink colour persists for about 30 seconds.
4. Repeat until two concordant readings are obtained. A potentiometric end point may be used instead of the indicator.

## Observations and calculation

| Reading | Weight of sample (g) | Burette initial (ml) | Burette final (ml) | Volume used (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | | | | |
| 2 | | | | |

Percentage purity = (V × molarity factor × 20.63 × 100) / (weight of sample in mg), where V is the volume of 0.1 M sodium hydroxide used and the molarity factor is (actual molarity / 0.1).

**Worked example.** Sample 0.5025 g (502.5 mg); titre 24.3 ml of 0.1 M sodium hydroxide. Ibuprofen found = 24.3 × 20.63 = 501.3 mg. Percentage purity = (501.3/502.5) × 100 = **99.8%**.

## Result

The sample of ibuprofen contains ___ % w/w of C13H18O2 (the pharmacopoeial limit is given in the current monograph, normally not less than 98.5% and not more than 101.0% on the dried basis).

## Precautions

1. Neutralise the alcohol before dissolving the drug; alcohol often carries traces of acid, which would give a high result.
2. Dissolve the sample completely before titrating, since undissolved particles react slowly and the end point creeps.
3. Add the titrant slowly near the end point and accept the first permanent pink.
4. Keep the flask stoppered between readings to limit loss of alcohol and entry of carbon dioxide.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is alcohol used as the solvent?** Ibuprofen is practically insoluble in water but freely soluble in alcohol, which takes no part in the reaction.
2. **Why must the alcohol be neutralised first?** Any free acid in the solvent would consume sodium hydroxide and be reported as drug.
3. **Why is phenolphthalein suitable?** The titration is of a weak acid with a strong base, so the equivalence point is on the alkaline side, where phenolphthalein changes.
4. **Which enantiomer of ibuprofen is active?** The S enantiomer inhibits cyclo-oxygenase; the R form is largely converted to S in the body, and the marketed drug is the racemate.
5. **To which chemical class does ibuprofen belong?** The arylpropionic acids, which also include naproxen and ketoprofen.
6. **Name another method of assay for ibuprofen.** Ultraviolet spectrophotometry and high performance liquid chromatography, which are also used for its formulations.

# Assay of aspirin

**Aim:** To determine the percentage purity of aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) by back titration after alkaline hydrolysis.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your own lab manual, the current Indian Pharmacopoeia monograph and your teacher where they differ.

## Principle

Aspirin is both an acid and an ester. If it were titrated directly, only the free carboxyl group would be measured. In the official method an **excess of standard sodium hydroxide** is added and the mixture is boiled: one molecule of alkali neutralises the carboxylic acid and a second hydrolyses the acetyl ester, giving salicylate and acetate. The unused alkali is then **back titrated** with standard acid.

```text
Step 1  CH3COO-C6H4-COOH  +  NaOH        →  CH3COO-C6H4-COONa  +  H2O
Step 2  CH3COO-C6H4-COONa +  NaOH  (heat) →  HO-C6H4-COONa     +  CH3COONa
```

Two moles of alkali are therefore used per mole of aspirin, so **each ml of 0.5 M sodium hydroxide is equivalent to 45.04 mg of aspirin** (molecular weight 180.16, half of it per mole of alkali).

## Requirements

Aspirin sample, 0.5 M sodium hydroxide (standardised), 0.5 M hydrochloric acid (standardised), phenolphthalein solution, conical flask 250 ml with a reflux or air condenser, water bath, burette, analytical balance.

## Procedure

1. Weigh accurately about 1.5 g of aspirin into a 250 ml conical flask.
2. Add exactly 50.0 ml of 0.5 M sodium hydroxide from a pipette or burette.
3. Fit an air condenser and boil the mixture gently on a water bath for about 10 minutes to complete the hydrolysis; then cool to room temperature.
4. Add 2 to 3 drops of phenolphthalein; the solution is pink because alkali remains.
5. Titrate the excess alkali with 0.5 M hydrochloric acid until the pink colour just disappears.
6. Carry out a **blank**: repeat steps 2 to 5 without the sample, so that any carbonate in the alkali is allowed for.
7. Repeat for concordant readings.

## Observations and calculation

| Reading | Weight of sample (g) | 0.5 M NaOH added (ml) | 0.5 M HCl used (ml) | Volume of NaOH consumed (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | | 50.0 | | |
| 2 | | 50.0 | | |
| Blank | — | 50.0 | | — |

Volume of alkali consumed by the drug, V = (blank titre − sample titre) in ml of 0.5 M hydrochloric acid, which is numerically equal to the ml of 0.5 M sodium hydroxide used.

Percentage purity = (V × molarity factor × 45.04 × 100) / (weight of sample in mg).

**Worked example.** Sample 1.5020 g (1502.0 mg); blank titre 50.0 ml; sample titre 16.6 ml; both solutions exactly 0.5 M. V = 50.0 − 16.6 = 33.4 ml. Aspirin found = 33.4 × 45.04 = 1504.3 mg. Percentage purity = (1504.3/1502.0) × 100 = **100.2%**.

## Result

The sample of aspirin contains ___ % w/w of C9H8O4 (the pharmacopoeial limit is given in the current monograph, normally not less than 99.5% and not more than 101.0%).

## Precautions

1. Add the alkali accurately; the whole assay depends on knowing exactly how much was taken.
2. Boil long enough for complete hydrolysis, but keep the condenser fitted so that nothing is lost by evaporation.
3. Cool before titrating; a hot solution gives a drifting end point with phenolphthalein.
4. Always run a blank with the same alkali, since carbonate in the sodium hydroxide affects the result.
5. Store aspirin in a dry place; it hydrolyses on standing in moist air, which shows as a smell of acetic acid and a positive ferric chloride test.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is a back titration used instead of a direct one?** A direct titration would measure only the free carboxyl group; the back titration measures the ester as well, which is what the monograph requires.
2. **How many moles of alkali react with one mole of aspirin?** Two: one neutralises the acid and one hydrolyses the ester.
3. **Why is phenolphthalein chosen?** The final titration is of a strong base with a strong acid in the presence of weak acid salts, and the colour change on the alkaline side suits this system.
4. **How can free salicylic acid in the sample be detected?** By the violet colour given with neutral ferric chloride solution; the monograph sets a limit for it.
5. **Why does the antiplatelet action of aspirin last about a week?** It acetylates cyclo-oxygenase irreversibly, and the platelet has no nucleus to make new enzyme.
6. **What is the purpose of the blank determination?** To correct for carbonate and for any acidity or alkalinity of the reagents and the glassware.

# Assay of furosemide

**Aim:** To determine the percentage purity of furosemide by titration in dimethylformamide with sodium hydroxide.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your own lab manual, the current Indian Pharmacopoeia monograph and your teacher where they differ. Dimethylformamide is harmful by inhalation and through the skin; work in a fume cupboard with gloves.

## Principle

Furosemide, 4-chloro-2-(furan-2-ylmethylamino)-5-sulphamoylbenzoic acid, carries a **carboxylic acid** group and a weakly acidic sulphonamide group. It is practically insoluble in water, so the assay is carried out in **dimethylformamide**, a basic solvent in which the acid is strengthened and dissolves completely. It is then titrated with standard **sodium hydroxide**, the end point being taken with bromothymol blue or, better, potentiometrically.

**Each ml of 0.1 M sodium hydroxide is equivalent to 33.07 mg of furosemide** (molecular weight 330.74, the carboxyl group being titrated).

## Requirements

Furosemide sample, dimethylformamide, 0.1 M sodium hydroxide (standardised, carbonate free), bromothymol blue indicator or a potentiometric assembly with a glass and calomel electrode, nitrogen supply, conical flask, burette with guard tube, analytical balance.

## Procedure

1. Weigh accurately about 0.25 g of furosemide and dissolve it in about 50 ml of dimethylformamide in a dry conical flask.
2. Pass a gentle stream of nitrogen over the solution to keep out carbon dioxide.
3. Add a few drops of bromothymol blue, or place the electrodes for a potentiometric titration.
4. Titrate with 0.1 M sodium hydroxide until the yellow colour changes to blue, or to the inflexion of the potentiometric curve.
5. Carry out a blank titration on the same volume of dimethylformamide and subtract it.
6. Repeat for concordant readings.

## Observations and calculation

| Reading | Weight of sample (g) | Burette initial (ml) | Burette final (ml) | Volume used (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | | | | |
| 2 | | | | |
| Blank | — | | | |

Corrected volume V = (titre − blank), in ml.

Percentage purity = (V × molarity factor × 33.07 × 100) / (weight of sample in mg).

**Worked example.** Sample 0.2510 g (251.0 mg); titre 7.8 ml; blank 0.2 ml; titrant exactly 0.1 M. Corrected volume = 7.6 ml. Furosemide found = 7.6 × 33.07 = 251.3 mg. Percentage purity = (251.3/251.0) × 100 = **100.1%**.

## Result

The sample of furosemide contains ___ % w/w of C12H11ClN2O5S (the pharmacopoeial limit is given in the current monograph, normally not less than 98.5% and not more than 101.0% on the dried basis).

## Precautions

1. Use dry, neutral dimethylformamide and run a blank, since the solvent itself is slightly acidic on storage.
2. Keep carbon dioxide away from the carbonate-free alkali; use a guard tube on the burette.
3. Dissolve the sample completely before titrating.
4. Protect furosemide from light, as it is light sensitive and discolours.

## Viva questions

1. **Which group of the molecule is titrated?** The carboxylic acid group; the sulphonamide group is much weaker and is not titrated under these conditions.
2. **Why is dimethylformamide used?** It dissolves the drug and, being a basic solvent, strengthens the weak acid so that a sharp end point is obtained.
3. **To which class of diuretics does furosemide belong and where does it act?** It is a high-ceiling (loop) diuretic acting on the sodium-potassium-two-chloride carrier in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.
4. **What is the chemical relationship between furosemide and the sulphonamides?** It is an anthranilic acid derivative carrying a sulphamoyl group, a development from the sulphonamide diuretics.
5. **Why is a blank determination necessary?** To correct for acidic impurities in the solvent and for dissolved carbon dioxide.
6. **Name an important adverse effect of this drug.** Hypokalaemia, along with dehydration, hyponatraemia, hyperuricaemia and, with rapid high intravenous doses, ototoxicity.
